subtopic: RECOGNITION BY ALLIED GOVERNMENTS- CONSULTATION WITH CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RECOGNITION BY ALLIED GOVERNMENTS- CONSULTATION WITH CANADA
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has Canada joined in the recognition of the government of Marshal Badoglio and King Victor Emmanuel in Italy? Has the government been consulted in regard to such recognition, or if not, has the government voiced any disapproval of such recognition?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RECOGNITION BY ALLIED GOVERNMENTS- CONSULTATION WITH CANADA
speechtext: My hon. friend gave me a copy of his question and I shall reply. At the time of the surrender of Italy, September 8, 1943, the royal Italian government was recognized by the governments of the united nations as the responsible government to conclude the Italian armistice. It has subsequently been recognized by the allied governments as a co-belligerent. Canada was consulted about the recognition of the Italian government for these purposes, and approved.

speechtext:
On Monday, February 28, I directed certain questions to the Minister of National War Services in regard to the control and censorship of news commentators, and in particular Mr. Philpott in reference to the McNaughton case. The minister undertook to give me a reply. I brought up the matter again a day or so later. Is the minister in a position now to give me an answer to these questions?
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): I brought some information to the house this afternoon, but the hon. member for Lake Centre asked this question before I had the opportunity of giving him the information he asked for the other day. I wish to table a copy of Mr. Elmore Philpott's week-end review of February 20, 1944.
In regard to the matter of censorship, I have looked it up and I shall read into the record directive No. 1, to be found in the censorship directives handbook which was tabled in this house on January 28, 1944. It is headed "Onus of Responsibility," and is as follows:
Broadcasters are reminded that the full' onus of responsibility for observance of the defence

National Flag
of Canada regulations, in so far as they affect radio, is vested in them. To this end, every precaution should be taken to safeguard against the broadcast of any information likely to help the enemy, or inimical to the national interest. Irrespective of their position or function, all speakers should be fully familiarized with the censorship restrictions now or hereafter in force.
Broadcasters in all categories should be thoroughly conversant with the censorship requirements in order that all danger of violation may be reduced to an absolute minimum.
Information was sought also on the point of "the limitations short of censorship placed on the commentator." I find nothing explicit in that connection. But I understand that the limitations are those of good taste and good judgment, and, of course, observance of any C.B.C. regulation which may be applicable to any case in point.
I am advised that the script in question was not sent to Ottawa. I surmised that the other day; I now confirm it. I am told that no one in Vancouver read through Mr. Philpott's script before it was broadcast.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my purpose to hold up the estimates of the department, or to deal with them in as great detail as has been my practice in other sessions. I observe with interest, of course, that these estimates are substantially larger than they have been in other years. I can recall that not so many years ago the agriculture estimates were little more than a third as large as they are at the present time; and in addition to what has been spent on agricultural services, as was pointed out not long ago in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Haldimand, in the last two or three years we have spent on Canadian agriculture something approaching a quarter of a billion dollars. It may be said, and with some truth, that much of this money has had to be spent because we have not progressed as far as we might have in connection with scientific agriculture, or indeed because we have never had an over-all national agricultural policy. It has been a more or less haphazard policy, and now we seem to be paying the penalty. Just to what extent bonuses and subsidies will have to be carried on is not known even to those who may feel optimistic of the support that has been given to agriculture during these difficult years.
I notice that included in the estimates is some $50,000 or $75,000 to be spent by the entomological branch for the protection of forests, which I suppose would include the distribution of insecticides to deal with all sorts of forest diseases, and I wish to draw the committee's attention to the relative importance of the forest industry of this country and to indicate what little attention has been given it in this parliament. I think I can say that during the last twenty years the estimates of the Department of Agriculture have been more thoroughly discussed than those of any other department of the government. On many occasions we have discussed wheat; we have dealt with live stock and dairy products, plant diseases and everything else that comes under this department. I believe that in many cases the money spent by this department has been spent wisely, but I do not believe the estimates of any other department have received anything like the attention and discussion that parliament has given the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. On the other hand
*Mr. Mackenzie King.]
we have all the great industries associated with our forest resources, to which we have given no attention in years gone by and on which very little money has been spent. I suggest to the minister that the government should give some consideration to the reorganization of the various services involved, to the end that the great forest industry of this dominion may be given more national attention.
We look at the estimates and find that all the forestry services furnished by the federal treasury cost a total of only about $300,000. This is only thirty per cent of what is spent annually on our national parks. Then we see that $1,875,000 annually is spent in order to provide the services of the fisheries department. I know 'the Minister of Fisheries will not want that amount reduced, nor will the fishermen throughout this dominion, because it is a very valuable resource which I believe produces some $50,000,000 to $70,000,000 annually for that industry. On the other hand the forest resources of Canada return to this country's treasury approximately $79,000,000 in tax revenue alone each year, of which less than one-half of one per cent is spent in the protection and conservation of our great forest wealth.
During the last few weeks we have done a good deal of talking about the post-war period. Indeed, it has seemed to me that we spent a great deal of time talking about post-war rehabilitation problems when we should have been spending more time considering how to win this war, because it is not won yet. With the single exception of agriculture no industry contributes more to the favourable trade balances of this country than does the forest industry; none produces more of the things necessary to carry on the war; none contributes more to the employment of our people. To-day the products of our forests are contained in the parcels that go to the battle fronts, in the waddings used in the hospitals, and in hundreds of new commodities which have been developed during the last five years. Long ago Germany and other countries which are now our enemies planned constructive forestry policies and gave their great forest resources a prominent place in their national considerations. speechtext:
I think I am still in order when I recommend that the Minister of Agriculture take the forest service entirely out of his department. I refer to the surveys with respect to insects carried on by his department. I would suggest, too, that two or three pages of the report of his department referring to that subject could then be deleted. If we cannot discuss this matter under the estimates of this department, then I think there should be a reorganization in order that this problem can be more fully considered. Surely we would be in order as a committee to discuss the advisability of taking out some of the service items that are now in these estimates and placing them, if you will, under the Department of Mines and Resources w'here I think they should be.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has mentioned that there are emergency problems, but I would point out that this matter is an emergency problem. We must realize the great damage that has been done during the last four or five years. We should endeavour to arouse this committee to arriving at some solution or making a greater effort than the small effort being put forth to-day. I am merely pointing out that the services having to do with this great primary industry should be solidified and consolidated under one department. Something should be done along that line.
As I suggested at the outset, the minister must share at least a part of this responsibility with the Minister of Mines and Resources. Neither department is doing very much, nor has much been done in the past. I am laying this matter on the doorstep of the government, because it is their responsibility; but it must be admitted that for the last seventy years very little has been done for this great primary industry, which has grown to be the most important in this dominion; employs the most

Supply-Agriculture
labour, and produces a greater favourable trade balance than any other industry. It has made to the mother country an important contribution to the war by providing over a billion and a half feet of lumber per year. It has given assistance to our friends in the United States by assisting in their requirements for explosives, for alcohol, for glycerine and many other things made from these products. Yet for seventy years this industry has been allowed, to grow up almost like Topsy so far as national direction is concerned. During the last twenty years problems have arisen which I submit create an emergency now. They should be dealt with before next spring. There is the spruce bark beetle, the bronze birch borer, the budworm, the jack pine sawfly and mountain pine beetle. Hon. members from British Columbia know the damage that these insects are doing. Every part of this dominion is affected. I know it has been said that we cannot deal with these matters because the provinces have autonomy over their own civil and property rights, but I submit that this government should review without delay the possibilities of establishing a national forest policy to cooperate with the provinces.
Some department should be made responsible for preventing the terrific losses we have sustained. From 1878 to 1886 very large quantities of the accessible timber in the state of Maine and the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick were destroyed. The preponderance of balsam since that time has made our forests more vulnerable to the spruce bud-worm. From 1910 to 1920 from forty to sixty per cent of the accessible spruce and balsam in the state of Maine and in large sections of Quebec and New Brunswick was affected by this insect. The present budworm infestation began in the district north of Sudbury in 1935 and 1936. Foresters in that district claim that because of this infestation there was more damage by fire in two days in 1941 than there had been in the previous ten years-the ravages of the budworm making the trees so much more susceptible to fire hazards.
An estimate made by the best forestry authorities in the dominion indicates that this budworm infestation now threatens 45,000 square miles. The area damaged spreads through Ontario, Quebec, and part of New Brunswick, and over 15,000 square miles of forests are already destroyed. Do hon. members realize what that means The minister's report states that 40,000 square miles are seriously affected. This represents the destruction of 50 million cords of wood, or sufficient pulpwood to keep the pulp and paper mills of this country going for thirty-five years. Yet the federal government and this parliament have done practically nothing about it.
As has been stated by the leading entomologists in this country, we are twenty years behind the times in our effort to overcome this devastating budworm menace. Other countries have national policies in connection with their great resources. We talk a lot about rehabilitation, about free money, about giving pensions, about finding places for our men, and very little about conserving and preserving and developing our own resources, which are so fundamental to our great primary industries. It is upon these industries that much, of our national wealth and national employment and national prosperity depend. It is true that something has been done, but it touches only the fringe of the problem. From 1909 to 1920 over 200 million cords of spruce and balsam pulpwood were destroyed in Quebec and the maritime provinces by the spruce budworm.
This problem transcends the borders of the dominion; it affects the United States of America as well. On two or three occasions the state of Maine has suffered great loss. I am glad to note that there is a bill now before congress which will provide large sums for investigation and research work in an effort to arrive at a solution of this problem. Many things have been tried. Because of the nature of the problem, dusting by aeroplane has not proven entirely successful, but there is no doubt that much can be done through proper forest management, protective service and cooperation between the provinces and the dominion.
We have not faced this problem, and we must face it in order to arrive at a solution. We cannot sit idly by and watch what is happening. Every infestation affects millions of cords more than the previous one. We have been warned repeatedly during the last quarter century by the leading entomologists that unless something is done, resources of great value will be lost to the dominion. True, when you look over the map you can see enormous areas of timber still in Canada; but remember, our resources are not inexhaustible. We have excellent yellow birch in the far east, stately firs in British Columbia, and large white pines in this old province, much of which, however, has been exploited, and now we have left in its place a growth of balsam, which is fertile ground for the budworm to do its work.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that we certainly have not met this problem. There is no industry which gives more employment in Canada to-day or has more capital invested in it than the allied forest industries, and they depend entirely on the raw production from these great forest areas. I believe that there is more hope for employment after the war

through new uses of wood products than there is in any other single industry in Canada, but that industry is dependent upon the accessibility of sound timber. After the war we shall have to compete with Sweden and Finland and even Russia, and therefore I think it is fitting under our good neighbour policy that we take this problem up with the United States of America. I ask the government of the day to face this problem and see if we cannot bring about some joint cooperative effort between Canada and the United States to deal with it. It is not only a provincial or a dominion problem, but from its very nature it is as well an international problem. If a great forest fire starts in the Gatineau, we soon know it down here because we smell the smoke. But until we are almost on fire ourselves we do not seem to wake up. Insect infestation can prepare vast areas of our forests, square mile after square mile, in one year for a forest fire. The fallen timber through insect infestation creates a fire hazard and now causes greater annual destruction than all the timber cutting itself in this dominion.
Eemember, the figures I have given are not small figures. Forty thousand square miles is a large territory, and 15,000 square miles is now a fire hazard and a prey for the fungi and insects to which I have referred.
It does seem to me that excuses such as provincial rights should not brush aside this problem. We must grapple with it in a national way, establish surveys and detection services, international in scope, and enlist the joint efforts of the federal bureaux of entomology and plant pathology in an endeavour to solve it. It is true that we have made certain strides forward in the distribution of insecticides and parasites, and there has been more research into control methods. We have a laboratory at Belleville. The Imperial Institute has been moved out from England for the duration, and is doing excellent work. It has been shown, that parasites can be produced in sufficient numbers to be spread over areas in such volume as to prevent this insect infestation, if the work is done in time. But they cannot be spread over 15,000 square miles, and many entomologists are agreed from past experience that this work must be done in time if the forests are to be saved. And so I say, Mr. Chairman, that we must have surveys made and detection services set up. I leave it to this house to say, no matter whether the problem comes under this department or not, whether we are giving the necessary attention to this great national resource, a resource that brought to this country in 1941 alone a production of 1537,000,000 worth

and a favourable trade balance of $350,000,000. It is an industry which directly and indirectly is supporting over half a million of our people.
The question is important from many other angles as well, of which hon. members are no doubt familiar. There is the effect upon our climate and upon soil erosion. We spend a lot of time in the' different provinces in discussing reforestation policies. I can well remember the time, a quarter of a century ago, when reforestation was started by our county councils, and in Simcoe county, where I live, we have been reforesting ever since and now have substantial reforestation areas. But it takes a long time to reforest 15,000 square miles, and mother nature has proven to be the best reforestator we have yet seen. Again I repeat, we have wilfully neglected the great major national resources of this dominion. It seems to me that we, the representatives of the people in this house, should urge upon the government that more time and effort be spent on national research and the development of these resources and on their conservation and wise and scientific utilization. If we spend more time on these vitally important matters and less time on some of the wild dreams some people have of giving people something for nothing, it will open the door to opportunities and restore the confidence necessary not only to industry but especially to the labouring man himself. Nature has blessed us with timber resources in greater abundance than those possessed by any other people. Surely we should not fritter them away. I hope that the history of the next seventy years will not be a repetition of the last seventy, in which we have recklessly neglected an important obligation which rests right on the shoulders of this government-

A great many farmers have only a small acreage in wheat; perhaps fifty per cent of them have less than fifty or sixty acres, and those farmers were not protected at the very low prices we were getting and the quota we had to have. I am not quarrelling with the quota, because it was necessary, but one year it was paid on only three bushels to the acre, at 70 cents a bushel. Imagine what a farmer could do with that amount of money in paying his threshing gang, buying twine and so on.
Now I come to what I suggested to the government. I realized that we had a surplus of wheat in Canada and that the price could never go up until we either got rid of that surplus or at least substantially reduced it. At the same time I realized we had not a market for all our wheat, but we had one for a certain portion of it. I argued that if the government would come out boldly and say to the farmers of Canada, "We can sell 280,000,000 bushels of your wheat. We will pay you a fair price for it per bushel, and if you wish to grow more wheat, you can take care of it yourselves," we would have rid ourselves of paying for the storage of millions and millions of bushels, storage charges paid to the elevator companies of this country, including the pools. I know someone will mention the pools. That has been done before, so I will say, "including the pools." I argue that if the government had paid us a fair price, a price which most of us agreed should have been about a dollar a bushel, they would not have needed the wheat reduction bonus. Let me remind the committee that I am criticizing only that one bonus, namely the wheat reduction bonus. Some of the other bonuses, especially those provided under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, command a great deal of respect from me. I believe there are great possibilities in that measure, and it should be continued in operation. And yet there are dangers, may I tell the Minister of Agriculture. I repeat that
there are dangers in that act, because if we persist in paying farmers to grow wheat on land which should be in grass, then we are doing an injury to our country, and injury to the farmers who stay on that kind of land.
Yes, a fair price for the wheat, and we would have got away from that bonus. We could have built our granaries on our farms. Possibly I should have said at the outset that for two years farm storage was paid to the farmers, and was then discontinued. If we had been granted the storage charges paid to the elevator companies, we would have had that money. The farmers could have built their granaries and the government would not have been out one cent. They would have got it all back. But, while that was the policy of the United States, it was not the policy of this government. I shall not go into further detail in that regard.
May I commend the government upon its anti-inflation policy? Certainly it is necessary to hold down the prices of farm products. Where would they go, if we did not have set prices for them? They would rise to the price levels in the United States. I am dealing particularly with wheat and coarse grain. The result was that we had to have some control over prices. By that action undue inflation was prevented. Farmers are just as keen as any other class of people in their desire to prevent inflation, and I now commend the government for its action in that regard.
May I compliment the Minister of Agriculture, too, upon the long-term agreements he is endeavouring to make. I have in mind particularly the four-year hog contract with the old country. Whether the terms have been finally agreed upon, I cannot say; but the endeavour is well worthy of commendation.
May I compliment the government, too, for the inference contained in the speech from the throne with respect to the setting of floor prices on farm products. That is a splendid undertaking. Nothing will give the farmer more confidence than the knowledge that when the war is over he will be able to realize from the sale of his products at least the cost of production-at least, I say, the cost of production. I should add that if he is to continue in business he is entitled to a fair margin of profit above that cost of production. That is a hope which we may carry with us, and we trust that that will be the government's policy. But if those floor prices are not adequate they will be of no use to the farmers. I believe it was the federation of agriculture that suggested that the present ceiling prices on coarse grains should be the floor prices to continue after the war. I shall not argue the

We thought that was a reasonable procedure to take. And, by the way, I had expected the minister to say, "You are getting the bonus." But there is the trouble; there was a delay of three or four months before the announcement came with respect to the extra three dollars on grade A and two dollars on grade B-l. Meantime we heard, although statistics now 
prove differently, that thousands of sows and immature hogs were being sent to the stock yards, because barley and oats were worth more when sold as grain. That was the situation. Is there not some other way of doing business, some way which will not upset the equilibrium?

speechtext:
I should like to take up with the minister one or two matters which probably involve two departments, because we have production under the Department of Agriculture and marketing under the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have been receiving letters from farmers in the west during the past few days pointing out that they think the government should guarantee a fair floor price on oats and barley, otherwise they will seed their entire acreage this year to wheat. Some of these farmers will begin seeding operations in a month's time, and they should know what they can expect as a floor price on coarse grains.
I know there is a price now, but I think the floor price should be what it is now plus the bonus referred to by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, although he did not call it a bonus. This would give the farmers a return far below the prices prevailing in the United States. I put some figures on Hansard on February 1 when I was speaking in the debate on the speech from the throne. The

Supply-Agriculture
government should be able to give the producers some assurance as to what they can expect as a floor price on coarse grains. If that is not done our whole programme of production will be disrupted and we shall be disappointed in the acreage sowed to oats and barley in many sections of the west.
The next matter I should like to refer to has to do with flax. The government have announced that they will pay $2.75 per bushel for flax grown this year. In my opinion that price is not satisfactory, and this is borne out by what has been said by many who are more conversant with the matter than I am. The government itself realize that this is the case because in the quarterly review on Canadian coarse grains dated February 14, 1944, they point out in connection with flax:
-a further increase of 500,000 acres took place. A new high was established in 1943 when 2,947,000 acres went into flaxseed.
Maintenance of the 1943 level of acreage in 1944 was the objective presented at the dominion-provincial agricultural conference last December, but a much lower acreage in 1944 was indicated for the west, especially by the representatives from Saskatchewan. It is believed, however, that the figure which emerged from the conference and which showed, a reduction of about 1,000,000 acres from the 1943 level as the probable acreage in 1944 is not acceptable to those charged with the wartime programme affecting fats and oils. Every effort will yet be made to repeat the 1943 flaxseed acreage this year.
The price of No. 1 C.W. flaxseed to the grower (basis Fort William) was raised to $2.50 per bushel as of August 1. 1943, an increase of 25 cents per bushel over the previous fixed price, and unlike wheat and coarse grain, this crop can be marketed without quota restriction.
The statement goes on further, but I shall not burden the committee by quoting it. During the past few days a meeting was held in Winnipeg of the national barley and linseed flax committee, and they recommended to the officials in Ottawa a price of at least $3.25 per bushel for flaxseed, in keeping with need and price relationship to the standard crops. Flaxseed is not an attractive crop to grow and should be worth two and one-half times the price of wheat. Mr. F. H. Lehberg, the technical adviser to the oils and fats administration, wants a supply of flax on hand in order to trade with the United States.
The government have admitted that they do not think they will get this production. I would point out that the guaranteed price in the United States is $3.05 per bushel in their; funds, which means approximately $3.35 in Canadian funds. There is quite a difference. If this production is essential we should have an enhanced price in order to get the desired production. In my part of Manitoba flax is
not grown extensively. Many of those who endeavoured to grow it during the last two or three years do not intend to do so under the present rules and regulations and the prevailing price. If it is essential I hope the government will reconsider the price.
These are important matters. The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Leader) said that he thought the producers in Canada should receive the same prices as are being paid in the United States. I have advocated on previous occasions that there should be no trade barriers between the united nations. There should be freer access to the markets of the united nations for goods which are essential to our war effort. The other evening it was announced that meat rationing would be abandoned for the time being, but I do not think this will prove a cure-all for the difficulties we are facing in the marketing of cattle. I have wondered why we do not have access to the United States market for our live stock, especially when we are fighting our battles side by side. It has been pointed out before that the margin is not great enough between feeder or stocker cattle and finished beef. Men cannot buy cattle and feed and make a profit with the spread that now exists.
There are also some minor difficulties in connection with hog marketing. I have suggested on previous occasions that because of the great increase in the production of live stock, especially hogs, we should have a live stock commission to look after marketing problems. I still hope the government will consider this matter. I repeat that I hope the government will be able to tell the producers of this country what they may expect as a floor price for the coarse grains they produce in 1944. Something will have to be done to encourage them to increase their flax acreage, and a few weeks hence will be too late for this information to be of any value.

speechtext:
There are several matters in connection with agriculture which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I should like to secure from him answers to several questions dealing with particular matters, as well as to some dealing with the situation in general.
With regard to the request of the hon. member for Souris that there should be an increase in the price of flax, apparently the view he expressed represents the views of the members of the legislature of Saskatchewan, for only a few days ago a resolution was introduced there requesting, among other things, that because of the hazards in flax production and the urgent need for oil, the, federal government should give immediate consideration to the desirability of increasing present guaranteed prices for flax and other oil-bearing seeds. I find that there is general support for the request which has been made by the hon. member.
On the question of farm income, farmers generally throughout Canada have had their hopes considerably raised by the government's promise that it intends to bring into effect a floor for farm prices. But legislation setting out farm floor prices will be ineffectual unless the parliament of Canada secures the necessary powers to pass such legislation. The general feeling and demand throughout the west, and throughout Canada, is, I think, that the most effective method of maintaining an increasing farm production through the establishment of price levels would be by 
stabilizing the floor prices at levels sufficient to guarantee to all producers returns comparable with those of persons engaged in other industries, to use the words of the resolution introduced in the Saskatchewan legislature. I should like to hear something from the minister in regard to this matter. The promise of a floor base for farm prices will mean nothing after the war, after the terms of the War Measures Act cease to be operative, unless there is either an amendment to the constitution as it now stands or enabling legislation passed by the provinces. I brought this matter up on one occasion previously'', and the minister in the ccmse of his reply merely touched the subject without going into it in any detail. All of us believe in the necessity of establishing farm floor prices, but a promise not made effective by legislation will remain but a promise, without being implemented.

speechtext: Does my hon. friend see any constitutional difficulty in the way of the government establishing floor prices by means of subsidies?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: At the moment I was not dealing with that particular phase, but it does raise an interesting question. What I was going to point out was that if the government in setting floor prices does not secure the support and cooperation of the provinces, then its legislation, while it will offer a promise of assistance to agriculture, will be ineffectual.

speechtext:
I am not going to ask the minister to deal with the legislation itself but would ask that he answer one question. Has the government secured the legal opinion of the Department of Justice to the effect that this parliament has the power to bring into effect such a system of basic farm prices effective after the conclusion of the war? If the minister gives that assurance, if he tells the house and the country that the Department of Justice answers that question in the affirmative, then a promise that is so looked forward to by the farmers of Canada may very well be carried into effect. But if that assurance is not given, this promise may be mere window-dressing. In answering, the minister does not have to disclose what the scheme will be or the nature of the legislation to be introduced. All I ask him to do is to bring hope to the Canadian farmer that the legal right, power

Supply-Agriculture
and jurisdiction rest in this parliament to implement a promise which holds out so much hope to the farmers of Canada as a whole.
I pass to another phase, and that is in connection with the plans for the future development of agriculture. I think Canada was greatly honoured in the appointment of the Minister of Agriculture as a member of the united nations food board. I think he has a great contribution to make there. This board met some months ago and made plans for the future, for the interconnection of north American food problems, for Canada's contribution in the production fields. According to the news item I have before me, the importance of Canadian food supplies made it "appropriate and desirable" that Canada be represented directly as a member of the board. This board was set up originally in June, 1942, to coordinate the prosecution of the war effort by obtaining a planned and expeditious utilization of the food resources of the united nations. I think the country has the right to ask for a report from the minister as to the stand Canada is taking on this food board, as to the plans that are being made for the correlation of food production in the United States and Canada. Canada contributed a billion dollars last year to mutual aid. How much of that billion dollars represented agricultural products? To what extent was the future market for Canadian farm products established by the fact that there was delivered under this scheme a large proportion of Canada's food production?
In the United States the farmer has been encouraged in the disposal of agricultural products by the assurance that his surplus production otherwise not disposable will be absorbed by the system of lend-lease. According to the figures I have, in the two years of lend-lease between March, 1941, and February, 1943, the United States expended more than 39,500,000,000 in connection with the administration of that vast and important organization for victory, and of this amount foodstuffs and agricultural products accounted for $1,449,064,000. That is to say, fifteen per cent of the total amount advanced for mutual aid went in the disposal of surplus agricultural products. I should like to secure a statement from the minister, and I think the country has a right to it, as to the policy of the government in the disposal of agricultural prod-its under the system of mutual aid. What proportion of the amount disposed of by mutual aid consisted of agricultural products and the like?
I pass to another matter, which has already been mentioned by the hon. member for
Souris. It is generally agreed now that a substantial surplus of beef will be on hand in Canada. Will the minister place before us something of the representations, if any, that have been made for the export of our surplus beef to the United States, for the removal of any embargo that there is to-day. What is being done in this direction? During the past few days I have had a number of letters from farmers, pointing out that it is difficult for them to market heavy beef at the present time, there being no market in Canada. Surely, when the United States and Canada can cooperate in a great united nations food production board, it should be possible so to correlate production between the two countries that any difficulties in the marketing of our beef might be removed at this time. I would ask the minister to enlighten the committee in this regard.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) mentioned the wheat acreage reduction policy and its discontinuance in the present year. I do not know what the situation is in Manitoba, but I have received a considerable amount of correspondence from Saskatchewan in regard to this matter, pointing out that, in view of the great need for coarse grains for live stock production and the furtherance of that programme, the wheat acreage reduction policy should be continued during the present year. The minister has already stated that it will not be, and I would appreciate it if he would tell the committee why this policy was so abruptly discontinued after many farmers had done their summer-fallow operations in 1943, believing that it would be in effect in 1944.
Furthermore, and this is something peculiar to my own constituency, under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act there is an area which the minister knows of near Bethune in which over a period of years the farmers have had little or no crop, and yet under the law as it now stands they are unable to get any assistance through that act. I realize that legislation cannot be brought down to cover every possible contingency and to meet individual cases; and while I am very much opposed to orders in council and to order-in-couneil government, there are occasions when orders in council may be utilized to protect the rights of individuals. There are a number of farmers in that area who for several years, while contributing year by year, are in a position where they are denied that payment, separated as they are by a valley from the township in which the prairie farm assistance allowance is paid. I would ask the minister to look into
Supply-Agriculture

the situation to the end that these farmers be given consideration in the payment of this allowance.
There is one other matter that was dealt with by the hon. member for Souris. Some months ago Mr. John Bracken came out in favour of the establishment of a board of live stock commissioners. To-day that is a matter of universal demand without regard to party considerations. We have asked for it in the interests of the live stock producers; my hon. friends in the C.C.F. have asked for it, and in the legislature of Saskatchewan a resolution has been introduced requesting the establishment of such a body with producer representation. That resolution was introduced by two Liberal members in the legislature. Would the minister be prepared to advise the committee as to what attitude the government is taking with respect to the establishment of such a board and whether the matter is now under consideration.
I shall now refer to the matter of releasing wire for hog and poultry fencing. I would point out that the farmers are asked to produce hogs and poultry, and yet no arrangements are made to secure for them a release of the necessary allotment of wire for the purpose. There was for a time an order in effect freezing nails and wire. That order remained in effect while threshing operations were taking place in the west last fall. The farmers could not get the necessary nails to build granaries at the time they required them. Later on, by the time a good portion of the threshing had been completed in many parts of the province, the order was lifted and a general supply of nails was made available. I trust there will not be a repetition of that situation this year, which was most serious in parts of Saskatchewan. The farmers were able to get the necessary lumber, but could not get nails and they found themselves in the position of having to dump the wheat on the ground. The fact that such a condition exists shows that there is not the necessary cooperation between some of these war boards and the Department of Agriculture. There is need even to-day for an increase in the supply of wire, and I would ask the minister to bring to the attention of the board which is in charge in that regard the needs of the farmers and to request from that board a release of further amounts for the purpose.
These are a few of the matters on which I think the committee and the country deserve enlightenment from the minister. They are brought forward, not in a spirit of partisanship but from a desire to direct to the attention of the minister such conditions as, in my

opinion, deserve to be brought to his notice. They should receive serious consideration immediately.

speechtext:
So far as beef is concerned, the suggestion is made that the committee ought to know something about the relationship of Canada's position to that of the United States. Hon. members of the committee know that prior to the war we had a trade agreement with the United States. That trade agreement still exists. It provided for our sending to the United States 193,000 head of beef cattle, weighing seven hundred pounds or more, in any particular year, provided we co.uld deliver that number with quotas divided up into four covering three-month periods throughout the year. Let me repeat, that provision is still in the agreement which we have with the United States, and that agreement has been extended from time to time. But in 1942 we found it impossible to feed our own people on the beef which was coming to market. Because of the limitations which were placed on the consumption of pork we found it impossible to feed our own people and at the same time supply the United States market with the quota which might have been supplied under the agreement. I should like to call this to the attention of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie who is not in his seat at the moment. The policy that he speaks so much in support of is the policy which is largely responsible for what had to be done. It is becoming a habit in the house and outside for people to criticize things that the government has done and then follow this
up with the statement: "I am a very strong supporter of price control". One cannot be a very strong supporter of price control as we have it in the Dominion of Canada and at the same time say that our price levels must be the same as they are in the United States. The price controls in the two countries are not the same. The situations governing the necessity for price control are not the same and therefore, of course, differences must exist.
That was true with regard to beef cattle. We had a price ceiling. We had a wage ceiling. There is a relationship between the wage ceiling and the price ceiling. If you permitted cattle to be sold in the United States on the United States price level of that particular time, then only one thing could happen. Not only would you not have any beef for sending to Great Britain, but you would not have enough beef to eat in the Dominion of Canada if you maintained your price ceiling. Therefore, one of two things had to be done. Either the policy which everyone seemed to be in support of had to be abandoned, or there had to be some Canadian attempt to control the marketing of beef. Accordingly it was determined that cattle would be kept on this side of the line as long as they were required here, and that if there were any surplus to be sent out of Canada, that surplus should be sent to Great Britain. That decision was not reached as a result of a discussion which took place on this side of the line only. It was a decision which resulted from discussions between the government of Canada and representatives of the government of the United States. It was thought inadvisable, for example, that the United States should import cattle from Canada and then lease-lend an equal poundage of beef to Great Britain.
When that statement is made some people say, "What about the arrangement that was made with Mexico?" Well, making an arrangement with Mexico is a little different from making an arrangement with Canada. Mexico is not a part of the British empire, and up to the present Mexico has an entirely different relationship to the war from that of either the United States or Canada. Therefore the United States people might accept an arrangement which is entered into as between Mexico and their own people and at the same time have reason to object to cattle coming from what is a part of the British empire into the United States and they in turn giving it to the British. The natural thing for those who are producing cattle in the United States to say is: if anyone is going to give or provide, under mutual aid to Great Britain, beef which is
Supply-Agriculture

purchased in Canada, then it ought to be the Canadian government and not the United States government that does it. Therefore the position is this. There is a complete understanding between the United States and Canada. There is no possibility of any misunderstanding regarding any relation to the trade agreement which was made before the war, as a result of what has happened up to date. The United States people understand the reason for it. They are in agreement with what is being done. I am not so sure that they might not suggest that it ought to be done if the Canadian government had not considered their position in the matter when the policy was announced.
That brings me down to the time when we found that there was a surplus of certain kinds of beef in Canada. I would remind the committee that since the house was in session last year an arrangement was made, and it was announced in the house. Under the arrangement the meat board of the Department of Agriculture can purchase beef. That arrangement was to the effect that when beef-not cattle-which was being sold on this market reached the floor or came within one-eighth of a cent of the floor, the meat board of the Department of Agriculture could purchase that beef and put it down for freezing in order to send it to Great Britain.
We have been operating under that understanding, I think since May of last year, and there was no necessity to purchase any beef under that arrangement until quite recently. A small amount was purchased before Christmas, I believe, and some has been purchased since that time; but in regard to creating a proper attitude in Great Britain toward the beef which is shipped from Canada the regrettable feature is that none of the higher grades of beef has been materially below the ceiling, in the form of either beef on the market or of cattle being marketed. The only beef that has been down to and below the floor is cow meat, and anyone who is familiar with the meaning of that term knows it is not the kind of meat we want to send to Great Britain in any volume. However, we have purchased some quantities of cow meat and meat from the lower grades of other animals and sent it to Great Britain, but we have not been able to purchase any of the higher grades under the plan which has been in existence.
Under that plan, in spite of all the discussion that has gone on in Canada in regard to people going out of the production of meat, the quantities coming onto the market have been increasing constantly; and it is not the lower grade hogs that have been coming on the market in greater numbers. As a matter
(Mr. Gardiner.]
of fact, the high grade hogs that are coming on the market have kept well up to the average for any period one might wish to take in connection with cur marketing. I think we are still getting upward of 100,000 hogs a week more than we got at the same time last year, and a reasonable proportion of those hogs are of the grades which produce bacon which is sent to Britain, As a result we have considerable stores of bacon. At the same time we have more of the lower grades of beef coming on the market than we can absorb, and we have producers who are concerned as to whether they should place higher grades of cattle on the market, in the fear that they might be called upon to take a lower price than they had anticipated. I do not think it can be shown that any considerable number of persons have had to take lower prices for beef this year than they took in the same period a year ago. There is the occasional individual, of course, who sold high on the market last year and low on the market this year, who can send in a statement showing that he did not get as much this year as he got last year; but the latest averages I have seen indicate that prices across Canada for cattle have been higher this year than a year ago. We know, however, from the figures in regard to storage and marketing that there is. and has been for some time, the danger that so many high-grade cattle will come on the market in the spring of this year as to cause loss to those who have produced them, through the prices for cattle and beef going down to the floor, or through our storages being filled to the point where it is impossible for the plants to handle and process that beef as it must be processed in order to be sent to Britain. So that the action of a few days ago was taken, and I do not wish to go into that in further detail at the moment.
I come back to the point raised a few moments ago by the hon. member for Lake Centre, the question of our relationship to the United States with respect to the particular matter of the marketing of cattle. One has only to read the accounts, of what has taken place in. the United States in order to understand the situation there. On all these matters we are in the closest possible communication with the countries concerned. As a matter of fact, we were in communication not only with the government of the United States but with the government of Great Britain as to what ought to be done or what could be done to best serve the purpose. To understand the situation in the United States it is necessary only to point to the fact that a few hours before we took our action on Tuesday evening of this week, the United States, knowing

Supply-Agiicullure
what we were expecting to do, took action themselves which indicated that they are having just as much difficulty in processing the meat that is coming to their plants as we are having in processing the meat that is coming to the plants of this country. In addition, they are having difficulties similar to ours in providing for the movement of meat from this continent to the other side in the quantities which are available here at the moment.
I need only recite these facts in order to make it apparent that it would be foolish for the Canadian government to reverse its policy at the moment in relation to the issue of permits. Up to the present the United States government has done nothing about the matter. The contract is as it was before the war. The understandings have all been maintained right through the picture. The United States understands why we have done what we have done, and our actions have been taken after consultation with them. If. under those circumstances we were to reverse our policy and say that we were not going to require permits for the shipment of cattle into the United States, or that requiring permits we were going to issue them immediately and allow our cattle to be shipped to the United States, at a time when they are experiencing just as great difficulty in connection with processing as we are, I need hardly suggest to the committee how the Americans would be justified in looking upon an action of that kind. It is not our intention to give them any reason to feel that we do not understand the difficulties of their position, just as we understand our own difficulties.
However, we are attempting to work out at the earliest possible date a plan under which we can send high-quality beef to Great Britain. The present intention is to work out a plan somewhat the same as that under which we have been operating in connection with bacon and ham. With a contract of some kind which will assure that shipping will be available to take whatever quantities of meat we feel can be shipped or ought to be shipped to Great Britain under the circumstances, we shall be able to assist in feeding the British population from surpluses we have here. We believe that if we are going to follow a policy of that kind it ought to be applied to the higher, rather than to the lower grades of meat. We were spending a considerable amount of money prior to the war in an effort to convince the British people that we could put a high-class of beef products on the British market. We were selecting some hundreds of cattle from time to time, and shipping them over to Great Britain in the form of baby beef. We were spending
money in order to do that, and in order to demonstrate that we in Canada could produce good beef. Even during a considerable period of time before the war started, we had been selling on the British market in competition with Scottish-fed beef, and competing at even better prices, sometimes, than the Scottish beef was bringing. But the smallness of the movement, and the fact that it was only an experiment rather than a commercial activity, led to the fact that we lost money in sending that beef over. But we were prepared to lose money in order to advertise the fact that good beef of that kind could be secured for any market which might exist in Great Britain.
Now that we have an opportunity during war time of doing two things at one time, namely, doing a patriotic act and supplying beef to Great Britain at a time when she needs it, I believe we should demonstrate to the British people that we can supply good meat, the very best of it; because, when the war is over, if we are producing as many cattle as we are producing to-day-and all of us hope we shall be-we shall be requiring sooner or later a market for about 300,000 head of cattle. If we are not able to find that market on this continent, there is possibly only one other place where we can find a market, and that is in Great Britain. Therefore I say that we should establish the fact that we can produce in Canada beef which will compare favourably with beef secured from elsewhere. That, I think, is a full enough explanation of the government's present position and policy in connection with the marketing of beef. I would repeat that those policies are being followed with the fullest possible understanding between the British and Americans, with regard to the whole position.

The main attack made by the official opposition upon me, as the minister introducing the policy, was that I had brought it in by way of regulation, and not by a bill. The measure was submitted to the committee on agriculture, if I remember correctly, and was finally recommended to the house and put into effect. Again it was made quite apparent that this could not be a permanent policy.
We have come to the conclusion that this is the time to discontinue the wheat acreage reduction payments. Our reason for that is,
I am sure, apparent to most farmers of western Canada. The contention was, at the time the policy was introduced, that we should not. be making acreage payments, but that we should be increasing the price of wheat-just as was stated a few moments ago by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. We said at that time what he has already said, namely, that there would be farmers in western Canada producing three or five bushels to the acre, and others producing thirty or forty bushels to the acre; and that if we were to attempt to assist farmers to carry over from (Mr Gardiner.]
one period to another, producing the crop which w'e wanted them to produce, rather than one for which, for the time being, we had no market, we ought to provide that payments be made on an acreage, rather than on a bushelage basis. More particularly was that so when we were asking them not to grow so much wheat, but rather to grow more oats, more barley, more feed crops and to produce more live stock. We felt we should not take that action by raising the price of the commodity we did not want, but rather should say that in lieu of that particular commodity we would prefer to make a certain payment on an acreage basis.
There has been only one condemnation I have ever heard, since the policy has been in effect, and since it has been found that 182,000 farmers took advantage of it. And now it should be recalled that there was never anything in the regulations which compelled anyone to take advantage of it. We simply said to the farmers, "Here is the condition: If you wish to grow wheat, you can grow it. The government will give you an advance. We will pay you an advance upon it if you deliver to the wheat board, and give you a participation certificate. Then, some day we will pay you the earnings from that wheat, if it [DOT]is sold for a higher price. If you can get by for any term of years under a system of that kind, then go ahead and grow all the wheat you like." Some people did that. We said to others, "If you require to have cash coming in week after week and month after month from something you have to sell, there is only one way we can guarantee that, namely; if you feed live stock. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a few matters regarding southeastern Alberta. That great district has suffered more severely perhaps than any other agricultural district in the last few years. It is true that away back in 1915 and 1916, later in 1928 and again in 1938 and 1942, there were reasonably good crops in the district, but good years come so seldom that they cannot be relied upon. Consequently people who have settled in that district have fallen upon very hard circumstances and have had a difficult struggle. When we know that the average precipitation in that district is around twelve inches a year, and last year as low as nine, whereas in the east the precipitation ranges from twenty-five to forty inches, we can realize what a hard time they have out there to make the land produce enough to provide even the barest necessities of life for the people who live in that locality.
In those dry districts wheat is the grain crop most likely to grow, and therefore seventy-nine per cent of the grain produced there is wheat. Also, as regards ranching and stock raising, the cattle rancher can do a little better than any other producer of live stock. During the years of depression restricted markets brought ruinously low prices. The drought was quite severe, so that even grass and trees could not grow; the soil drifted, and many of the other hazards of farming were so great that it was almost impossible for the people to keep off relief. Consequently many of them had to seek relief during those years.
I wish to appeal to the government at this time to be lenient in the collecting of the seed grain liens which were put on during those years of depression, because, while the principal has not changed, the interest has mounted until it is often more than the principal, and it is very difficult for these people to face that debt at the present time.
. In fact, the district has been called the Canadian desert, for away back in 1874 Colonel Walker, going through the district, said that during his whole life he had never seen a pasture field so lacking in feed as were the prairies at that time. But that district need not be a desert. On an experimental farm which this government started, 2,400 tons of hay were produced off an area which otherwise would not have provided fodder for one animal. This shows that the district can be improved, and the government has done a good deal to improve it by establishing community pastures, stock-watering reservoirs and dug-outs; and by planting trees, by regrassing
Supply-Agriculture

and by improving methods of farming. Thore is still much that needs to be done, however, because cattle and wheat are not the products that the market requires especially, nor are they the products which the health of the people of Canada demand. What is required is more in the line of dairy products, fruits and vegetables and commodities of that kind, and these people are entitled to have comfortable homes where they will have shelter belts, gardens, small fruit trees, flowers and so on, as well as water for poultry and live stock which they could keep around their homes.
So that in addition to the work done by the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, it is essential, if that great desert is to be reclaimed, that the larger irrigation projects be kept in mind. The department has published a little pamphlet, and I observe that the large irrigation scheme at St. Mary and Milk rivers is being considered. That scheme looks to the reclaiming of 345.000 acres at a cost of $45 an acre. In north Saskatchewan the William Pierce scheme looks to the reclaiming of 1,400,000 acres at a cost of S74.S9. There is one other scheme, however, and I cannot see why it should not be mentioned, because $13,000,000 of private capital has already been spent on it. That particular scheme contemplates the reclaiming of 200,000 acres on which government engineers are now employed, and which can be irrigated for about $20 an acre. I hope that the fact that it is not mentioned in the pamphlet does not mean that the government have given up the consideration of that scheme. May I ask the minister whether it does mean that this particular scheme has been considered unfavourably, because in this pamphlet the statement is made that the larger projects at St. Mary and Milk rivers and in north Saskatchewan are the ones being considered.
In view of the great possibilities for good which these large schemes represent, I suggest that, as soon as the war is over and labour and material are available, as a reconstruction project nothing would give more permanent results and bring greater blessings to the people than the reclamation of those desert areas.

I listened with a good deal of interest to the minister's statement before the evening recess respecting the wheat acreage reduction regulations. I believe those regulations have served a useful purpose in the past and, that purpose having been completed, I believe the government is wise in discounting the operation of the regulations, and in increasing the price of wheat. Any criticism I made in the past respecting those regulations was based upon the administration of certain sections, rather than against the principle of the regulations themselves.
We are assured in the speech from the throne that a floor price is being placed under agricultural products. No doubt the time to discuss that matter will be when the measure is before the house. In passing, however, I would say that when the floor is introduced it should be at a level sufficiently high to stabilize agricultural prices at a level based upon parity. However, a parity price alone would not rehabilitate agriculture on a permanent basis because, more than any other industry, agriculture faces tremendous hazards. Therefore I say it is most desirable that the government should introduce a comprehensive scheme of crop insurance.
The minister may feel that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is, in fact, a form of crop insurance. In reality, however, I think hon. members will agree it is nothing more or less than a form of drought relief. I am very much in favour of that act, and I am not criticizing it. The constituency I represent has benefited, owing to the fact that the greater portion of the drought area in Alberta is in my constituency.

Nevertheless the Prairie Farm Assistance Act cannot be considered crop insurance. A man who is farming in the west may suffer total crop failure after having contributed to the scheme for ten years, and then still not be eligible to benefits under the act, in any shape or form. In the house on earlier occasions the minister has taken the stand that a scheme of crop insurance would not be practicable. He has said that, as a-matter of fact, it would encourage inefficient farming.

The minister may deny that he criticized this on the ground that it encouraged poor farming, but I remember quite well in the past that one of the reasons he gave-

I wish to put the hon. member right on that. I have always taken the position that to attempt to put it on an individual farm basis, even the prairie farm assistance as we now have it, would tend to provide to keep people on sub-marginal land or to permit poor farmers getting assistance whether or not the weather had anything to do with their poor crops. That is entirely different from saying that the matter is one which could be brought within the powers of this parliament I am not giving that as my own opinion; that was the opinion I received at the time we brought forward this legislation. It was the opinion we received in all three of the prairie provinces.
In the early part of the century the request was made to bring in hail insurance as a federal measure, but it was stated at that time that the only legislatures having power to bring in hail insurance or any other kind of crop insurance were the provincial legislatures. In each of the provincial houses in western Canada hail insurance measures were brought in. That was a form of crop insurance. That is the position taken to-day.
When this measure was before the committee of the other house the then leader of the Senate, who was a very able lawyer, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, asked if I had consulted the Department of Justice as to whether this was ultra vires. I stated that I had and that they had given the opinion that 100-72
it was intra vires. The legal adviser to the committee, Mr. O'Connor, was present. He turned to Mr. O'Connor and asked for his advice. Mr. O'Connor stated that there was some question as to whether the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was not a form of insurance and he went on to indicate that if it were insurance it would be ultra vires. He then offered the further personal opinion that this legislation would be beneficial to western Canada and he thought it was worth while trying it out. I do not think the question whether the present legislation is ultra vires has ever been put to the test. This has been accepted as legislation favourable to those for whom it was provided, and as far as I know all of Canada has accepted the principle that assistance ought to be given. I repeat that the question of'whether we should provide insurance is a provincial matter. My understanding is that in at least one province they have a board or commission set up which is examining into a number of questions, including crop insurance. They realize that this is a provincial responsibility.

I think the minister will agree that any comprehensive scheme of crop insurance would be quite a large undertaking and perhaps beyond the means of a province to carry out. I hope that this question will be taken up at the next conference with the provinces. If the three western provinces are ready to agree to come under a scheme of crop insurance to be operated by the federal government, then the question as to whether or not it would be ultra vires would not arise. The scheme in operation in the United States has a great deal of merit. I have before me the annual report of the manager of the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation, which reads in part as follows:
The Federal Crop Insurance Corporation was created for the purpose of furnishing the wheat growers of the nation a form of protection that is offered by no other agency, governmental or private. In discharging its responsibility the corporation performs a great public service, a service of direct benefit to 1,380,000 wheat growers and, indirectly, to millions of others in rural and urban communities, as well as to the government itself.
I understand that every year the number of farmers taking out this insurance voluntarily has increased. The amount of acreage covered has not increased, but the number of farmers has. The plan of operation is as follows:
Under the wheat crop insurance programme a farmer may insure himself against loss in yield below seventy-five per cent or below fifty per cent, whichever he chooses, of his average yield. An insured farmer is protected against loss due to drought, flood, hail, wind, winter-kill, tornado, insect infestation, plant disease, and

other unavoidable hazards. No insured farmer is protected against loss due to negligence, malfeasance, poor farming practices, or from causes which he is in a position to prevent.
The last reference is to poor farming. I understand that in the United States committees are set up under the AAA which have the responsibility of seeing that farming methods are carried out on a satisfactory basis. It seems to me that their scheme has considerable merit. It has been extended beyond wheat, and other farm products are to be insured along similar lines.
I think the federal government should make a thorough examination of this scheme so that at the next conference with the provinces they may be able to discuss it and see whether the provinces would be ready to come under such a scheme on a national basvs. A scheme of this kind is beyond the financial ability of the provinces to handle satisfactorily. If such a scheme is put into operation without sufficient financial backing it will fail absolutely.	.

speechtext: Could the hon. member tell us the manner of payment and the amount of the premium under the scheme?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: The payment of the premium is made in wheat. Committees are set up which estimate the average yield of a piece of land over a period of years. The farmer then insures for either seventy-five per cent or fifty per cent of that average yield. Then he may either pay the premium in cash or give a note in payment. The premiums are worked out on an actuarial basis. In the fall any claim for payment may be met in wheat instead of in cash. When the farmer receives wheat he can sell the wheat under his quota and receive cash. The whole thing is done on the basis of grain. The premium may be paid in grain and any return from the insurance may be made in grain. It is up to the farmer to decide whether he wants to keep the grain or whether he wants to sell it.

Mr. NICHOJjSON : Although the minister is not making very rapid progress with his estimates, I think the general comments that have been made have been of such a nature that one might conclude that the farmers across Canada are not as much dissatisfied with agricultural policies as on former occasions. In my opinion the farmers of this country deserve a great deal of credit for having achieved such records of production in spite of the fact that they were dissatisfied until very recently with government policies relating to agriculture. They felt that there was no good reason why agricultural prices should be kept at such, low levels when the government was buying everything else on a cost-plus basis. But in spite of their dissatisfaction they have surpassed all previous records of production.

It has been demonstrated that we do not have to have foreign markets in order to produce large quantities of food and to give our people more bread, more milk, more cheese, more butter, and more bacon. It is interesting to note that we were able to ship to Great Britain in 1943 over 5,000,000 hundredweight of pork products as compared with 1,800,000 hundredweight in 1939; 98,000,000 bushels of wheat in 1943 as compared with 61,000,000 bushels in 1939; 868,000 hundredweight of fish as compared with 368,000 hundredweight in 1939; over 1,000,000 pounds of cheese as compared with 811,000 pounds in 1939; 40,000,000 dozen eggs as compared^ with 1,000,000 dozen eggs in 1939. In spite of these very large gifts, and everyone in Canada agreed that these gifts should be made to the people of Great Britain, who were making sacrifices such as we in Canada were not required to make, we were able to consume more milk ourselves, more cheese, beef, pork, chickens, potatoes, eggs, tomatoes and citrus fruits, as well as coffee and cocoa. We were short on butter and refined sugar and tea, but we actually consumed more pounds of these other commodities than we did in the year before the war. I think, therefore, that any administration in the future will find it difficult to satisfy the Canadian people that we cannot produce at least enough food to maintain a healthy nation in this dominion.
