I rather hesitate to take part in this debate to-night after listening to the remarks made by the chairman and by the minister. What I had in mind was more a discussion of general problems of agriculture and I thought that might come under administration as well as anywhere else. What prompted me, perhaps more than anything else, to say what I am going to say is that on February 18, the hon. member for Yorkton spoke for about forty minutes and he discussed the problems of agriculture, wheat, stock of all kinds and fruit and everything along that line. The hon. member for Yorkton painted what I would consider a very gloomy picture for agriculture. I do not think that is the proper thing to do. I believe that we should paint a picture for agriculture so that the boys we have on the farms to-day and the boys we have overseas fighting our battles will come back to the farms and remain in an industry that is something worth while.
As reported at page 644 of Hansard the hon. member for Yorkton spoke about the policies of the government. He concluded by saying, "It has failed entirely". I take exception to that, because I do not think there has been a government in a good many years that has done as much for agriculture as has this government. I believe the Minister of Agriculture, his officials and the government as well are to be congratulated upon what they have done for the farmers.
The hon. member for Yorkton went on to talk about wheat, the grain exchange and the packing plants. He spoke about the price of cattle and the price of cows. He complained that in the west they could get only 7i cents a pound for cows. I have two cows in my stable and last week I could get eight cents a pound for them. I think that is a good price for cows. I do not think there is any very great complaint about the price of 7J cents for cows at farms in the west. He then w'ent on to speak about fruit and the fruit growers of the Okanagan valley. He said that the price was so low it was not up to the cost of production. Well, I do know something about fruit. I think the apple growers in particular are well satisfied with the policies of this government, and with what this government has done for the fruit industry. We have had good prices this year for all kinds of fruit. The government have spent thousands and thousands of dollars on the fruit industry. They thought it was a
Supply-Agriculture

war casualty, and it was. They have spent thousands of dollars to protect the apple growers and to give them a decent break.
As I said before, I do not like to hear agriculture put on such a low plane. I have been a farmer all my life and I think that to-day there is no better job than farming. During the last five years the farmers have made a wonderful contribution to this war. They have done it with a scarcity of labour, a shortage of machinery and many other things. They are to be congratulated upon what they have done and the government are to be congratulated upon what they have done for agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture has been criticized all over this dominion. I have not always agreed with him. I have not any particular use for any man who is a yes-man. I think when you have an idea you should express it. Nor have I any more use for a man who is always finding fault, always criticizing. If we have criticisms to offer, we should offer them in a constructive way and try to be of some assistance to the government, especially in time of war.
The Minister- of Agriculture was criticized about the price of hogs at the time of the last agreement with Great Britain, because he suggested that the quota might be lowered and for, I believe, not increasing the price to S20 a hundred. At the time I said that the price should be more than it was. I think everybody agreed with that. But the minister announced the increase by bonuses and that has been of great help to the hog producers. If that had been announced at the time of the agreement it is possible there would not have been as many sows sent to market. However, that is not the only reason why sows were shipped to market. I know in Ontario we had the worst grain crop We have had in a great many years. That is the main reason why hogs were shipped to market in this province. A great many farmers would rather have 830 or $40 from their sows than pay $300 or $400 for grain, because they have not been used to doing that kind of business. ' There is the odd man in the business who does that, but the ordinary farmer in Ontario does not do it. What the government did in regard to freight assistance has been of great help to the eastern farmer. There is no question about that.
I was not too favourable to the coarse grain proposition when the minister brought it in some two or three years ago, but as far as Ontario is concerned it has turned out that we have the grain in years like this. As the

minister said this afternoon, it has cost $80,000,000 of the people's money to put that programme across. It might be money well spent.
The other night I listened to one or two members talking about the price of cattle and the spread that there should be between the price that the stocker would sell at and what one should receive for cattle. I can well remember that when I was a boy my father used to tell me he would need to have a profit of two cents a pound plus the gain on the steer if he was going to make any money. I have not followed that business very closely, but I think it is perhaps about right. However, I cannot see how any government can legislate for people in that business. I think they have to know their business, and not pay too much for their feeder cattle.
Then we heard the subject of wheat debated. Perhaps I am a little out of order now, but not any more out of order than some other hon. members have been. I believe the government is paying $1.23 or $1.25 a bushel for No. 1 western wheat at Fort William, plus participation certificates which may amount to anywhere from sixteen to twenty cents. In Ontario we are getting only SI.10 or $1.12 a bushel for wheat at the barn. I think something should be done. I do not know how many western members are going to rise and support the eastern wheat grower. It is true we do not produce very much wheat, probably twenty million bushels. In order to get participation certificates we have to export our wheat, which we do not do. I think some arrangement should be made whereby Ontario wheat should return $1.50 a bushel at the mill.
Then there is the question of fruit, eggs, cheese, butter and all other farm products. I was amused this afternoon when the hon. member for Souris said he was interested in the United States market. He thought we should still be shipping cattle across to the United States. It is not so very long ago, as I well remember, that we heard our friends of the Conservative party of that time saying, "No truck or trade with the Yankees. We do not want to have anything to do with them."

This afternoon there was a general discussion respecting floor prices. Did I understand the minister to say that legislation was being prepared to provide for floor prices, but that prices would be practically the

Supply-Agriculture

same as are paid now; that is, on oats and barley an addition of ten and fifteen cents respectively, and that for wheat the price would be practically the same as is now being paid by the wheat board?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: When we were discussing coarse grains I was not referring to floor prices. The hon. member for Souris asked me whether the present prices, plus subsidies of ten and fifteen cents, would apply on next year's crop. I stated to him that while this was a matter that really came under the Department of Trade and Commerce I was able to say without any hesitation that I did not think there is any intention that the return would be lowered for the crop to be seeded in 1944. But I did not discuss that in relation to floor prices. The bill with regard to floors which will be brought in will be in general terms. It will give authority to do certain things and those things will be done as the circumstances arise.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: The minister says he is quite certain they will not be any lower, but what interpretation is he putting on that?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
It is the interpretation which I gave this afternoon. Add the payment of ten cents a bushel to forty-five cents for oats and that gives fifty-five cents; add the fifteen cents a bushel to sixty cents for barley and you get seventy-five cents; then you take what can be obtained on the market. If you obtain the ceilings you would have 6-1/2 cents for oats and 4-3/4 cents for barley. Therefore, you could say that the prices could be up to seventy-nine cents for barley and about 61-1/2 cents for oats.
In addition there would be profits on sales made in the United States at prices higher than Canadian prices. The farmers would have participation certificates upon which they could draw additional earnings on oats and barley, provided the United States prices are higher and that a sufficient quantity is sold to counteract any sales made in Canada at the ceiling price and still give a profit. That is the present position, and I cannot conceive of there being any lowering of that position in relation to the crop to be seeded in the spring of 1944.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: Could the minister indicate at what price our barley is being sold in the United States? I understand they are paying SI.27.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
Our oats and barley
would be sold on the United States market at whatever prices are being paid there. Those grains are being sold on this market at the ceiling prices, and in the accounting the two

amounts received are put into a pool and spread over all the sales of oats and barley, both in Canada and in the United States. If there is anything left over and above the ten cents on oats and the fifteen cents on barley, it is paid to the farmers under participation certificates. Again I may say that we are discussing trade and commerce affairs.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: Who is doing the exporting, the wheat board or the exporters on the exchange?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: The grain exporters are doing the exporting, but it is being exported under permits given by the wheat board.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: The minister said he had covered my question in the answer he made to the hon. member for Souris. He dealt with coarse grains, and I should like to know if the same principle will apply to other commodities subsidized by the government. Is it the intention to include the subsidy in the floor price?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: I do not think those would be included in any arrangement for floor prices. I am simply saying that that is a position for next year. The provisions of the bill providing floor prices to be brought down, at which time all these matters may be discussed, will apply six months after the war is over. We are now working under the War Measures Act which will run until six months after the war, and the bill to be brought down will provide for activities following that time. We will then take action based upon the circumstances then existing.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
Since the Saskatchewan combatants have cooled off to some extent, perhaps I shall have a chance to Say a few words without getting into the family squabble. I am not going to discuss any particular phase of agriculture at this time, but I wish to say something about agriculture in general. We have heard a number of armchair farmers state this evening, and it has been said before, that the farmers are prosperous. Even some of our practical farmers have said that agriculture is better off to-day than it has ever been before. I want to show, if possible, that our farmers are not yet receiving anywhere near that to which they are entitled.
I think it is generally agreed that the farming population of Canada comprises about one-third of the total population. If we are to have fair play in Canada, then one-third of the population should receive approximately one-third of the national income. I do not know of any group that works harder or

Supply-Agriculture
longer hours than our farming population. I should like to give the percentage of national income which our farming population has received over a period of years, starting with 1926, one of our good years. The .figures are:
Year	Percent
1926		 17-8
1927		 16-4
1928		 17-6
1929		 14-6
This is the period which some of our economists have used in arriving at parity prices. During that time our farmers received an average of 16'6 per cent of the national income, or approximately one-sixth, when they were entitled to receive one-third. I do not think it is right to attempt to compute parity prices on that basis. Taking wheat as an illustration, if parity prices were in existence to-day we should be receiving not less than $1.41 or S1.42 a bushel. Since we were receiving only one-sixth of the national income at that time, I think the committee will readily agree that a price of $1.41 is much below what it should be if we are given that to which we are entitled.
We are told about the $80,000,000 which has been paid in bonuses. If we look back to the time when we were receiving seventy cents a bushel for No. 1 * northern wheat at Fort William, it would appear that we were losing not less than $200,000,000 on our wheat crop alone in one year. We are told also about the good prices which have prevailed since the present government came into office. My recollection is that in 1935 wheat was selling at 87i cents a bushel, and on one occasion since then it has gone down as low as seventy cents a bushel. Then a bill was brought into the house to pay sixty cents a bushel for No. 1 northern at Fort William. The fact that we are receiving $1.25 a bushel to-day for our wheat is not due entirely to the policies of this government. The war has brought about these present prices, and when we consider the cost in human life, it has been expensive indeed. Going back to the percentages of national income received by agriculture, I quote again:
Year	Percent
1929		 14-6
1930		   9-6
1931		 6-3
1932		 5-0
Our farmers are being criticized because they are in debt, and on occasion they have been charged with dishonesty because they do not pay their debts. If some of these armchair farmers or politicians can tell me how farmers can pa}' their debts when they are receiving
only five per cent of the national income, then I shall learn something very valuable. The figures continue:
Year	Percent
1933		 6-6
1934		 9-1
1935		 9-3
1936		 11-4
1937		 11-5
1938		 10-9
1939		 12-5
1940		 11-0
I am not giving figures beyond 1940, because that is when the war started. If agriculture is to be placed on a sound footing; if Canada is to be placed on a sound footing, then our farming population must receive a different deal. A rise of half a cent or one cent in the price of different commodities will not by any means correct the injustices that are being put over our farmers. I intend to speak of other agricultural matters as we reach other items, but for the time being I make these few remarks on behalf of Canadian farmers east as well as west.

There have been
articles, I think, in Time magazine, the Reader's Digest and some other publications of that kind which have put forth the idea that you could take a sugar beet seed, which is in clusters, break it up into individual parts and thereby sow just one seed where you now sow clusters, and thus reduce the labour in connection with the thinning of the plants. speechtext: Before we get too far away from the subject which the hon. member for Swift Current raised, the matter of sugar manufactured from sugar beets, I think it would be well to point out to the committee that in 1937 the beet sugar factories located in my constituency sold their sugar at four cents a pound. That sounds almost unbelievable, does it not? Yet in that year they made over $150 an acre for every acre in sugar beets that year. That sum of money was divided between the farmers and the manufacturer. I think that gives the lie to those who have maintained that the production of beet sugar in Canada is uneconomic. Then more recently the process which was mentioned by an hon. member has come into use, and several new types of labour-saving machinery have become available or are on the verge of becoming available, so that I think and in fact I am safe in saying I am sure the production of beet sugar in Canada will become an industry which we simply cannot afford to ignore. industry has become perhaps one of the greatest industries in Canada. On a previous occasion and again to-day the minister gave figures to show the rapid increase in poultry production in this country, and I think I am safe in saying that more difficulty is encountered in raising live stock than in any other branch of agriculture. Every year literally millions of dollars are lost to the farmers through different animal diseases. I suppose the minister will say that a large sum of money is provided under the health of animals branch for administration of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, but it seems to me that more could and should be done for the farmers of Canada from the point of view of research.
A number of animal diseases are prevalent in this country at the present time. First, we have tuberculosis which, however, has been eliminated to a certain extent and is pretty well under control. Then we have Bang's disease, which is causing great loss to our farmers. Unfortunately farmers very often try to hide rather than treat this disease. I understand that serums have been developed and that the policy of the department has been changed to permit the use of such serums, though only two, or three years ago they were not allowed, I suppose for obvious reasons. Even so, however, the manufacture of these serums is largely confined to small areas. I believe the Guelph agricultural college does produce serums for vaccination against Bang's disease, but I think this department might very well undertake the manufacture of such serums or at least see that they are manufactured in plentiful supply. Another bad disease which very much concerns live stock producers in Ontario is what is called shipping fever, or hemorrhagic septicaemia. Farmers buy cattle in the Toronto stockyard, or other places, and take them home for feeding. They must have those animals vaccinated right away, or they may suffer very serious loss, and in some instances that loss is suffered in spite of the vaccination. A farmer brings home a carload of cattle for which he has paid a good price, only to lose one or two from this disease, and I think something should be done to control this disease in the stockyards and in the cars in which these cattle are shipped. Then again we have nutritional diseases in swine; we have poultry diseases; we have parasitic diseases, sheep stomach worms and so on. I feel that I am giving the minister wise advice when I say that a great deal more money should be provided for research purposes along these lines. After all, the loss from these causes amounts to millions of

Supply-Agriculture
dollars, and I would ask the minister what is being done particularly in regard to Bang's disease and hemorrhagic septicaemia.

speechtext: Before the minister replies I should like to add a word to the observations made by the hon. member for Haldimand, who has brought up a matter of vital importance to the farmers of Ontario. Farming in this country would be made much easier if something could be done about the diseases which have been mentioned by the hon. member, but I should like to add to the list the disease of mastitis, which is causing the dairymen serious loss. I believe there are certain fields that might be investigated in connection with the control of that disease. Some serums have been used for a time and have appeared to be quite successful, but later they have been found to be of very little value. It seems to me one of the greatest hazards with which the farmer has to contend.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: That is, the dairy farmer.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
Yes. Then it seems to me that some research should be done in connection with pullorum, a disease which attacks poultry, and that a serum might be developed which would create immunity to this disease, because we know that certain flocks have become immune to it. The present method of having to blood test every chicken to find out whether its eggs should be retained is laborious work; but if a flock could be made immune it would mean a great deal to the farmer. I believe it to be a fact that pullorum can never be stamped out. Sparrows have it; pigeons have it, and they more or less mix with the farm flock, so that it would seem futile to try to eradicate the disease unless we are prepared to wipe out all the wild birds. I believe, however, that an effort might be made to develop a serum which would give immunity to the disease, and if that could be done it would be a great step in the right direction.
There is another matter to which I think the department should give some attention, namely, the protection of pure bred breeders in connection with a system of breeding which is becoming quite popular in many sections; that is, artificial insemination. This will lend itself to a great deal of fraud if something is not done to give authority to certain men to practise in this particular field. Many farmers assert that they can carry on this work just as well as anyone else. I believe, however, it should be confined to a certain number of people, so that they will have some authority to sign a certificate, thereby ensuring that the mating of those animals has not been done fraudulently, and so that there would be sires of calves which would set up a system of artificial insemination.

speechtext:
I should like to add my voice to those of other hon. members who have spoken with respect to the advisability of increasing or supplementing this important vote. To my mind it is a most important one. Our live stock industry has greatly increased, and with that increase there has been an advance in the incidence of disease among live stock. Among hogs in western Canada in the last two years, because of increased production we have found an increased development in disease. That disease may have been in existence before, but we had not had it on our farms. I know many farmers have become discouraged and are going out of hog production because certain diseases have cropped up. I believe that there should be more investigation and that any information the department has should receive wider circulation than it now receives.
In my view the circulation of such information might be done through municipal offices in western Canada. The people in those offices are interested in our farming population, and the information could be distributed through them. I would urge that there be more investigation in connection with hog diseases. There is a loss of from twenty-five per cent to thirty per cent in young pigs, and I believe that half of that might be saved if there were a little more knowledge on the part of people who are in production. It is a matter of being penny wise and pound foolish, if we do not have more work along this line, and have a greater distribution of information.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
I would first answer the question asked by the hon. member for Haldimand with regard to Bang's disease. This is a matter which has been discussed each year since I have been in the department. The story is simply one of advancement in treatment, and attempting to deal with the attack this disease has made upon cattle in Canada. It has been determined that the vaccination of calves during calf-hood, particularly if they are vaccinated at from four to six months of age, gives a considerable amount of defence against invasion of the causative organism of Bang's disease. This is being made use of in a practical manner in controlling infectious abortion. It can only assist and will never replace sanitary measures.
Along with this comes the question of the possibility of vaccinating mature cattle with strains of low virulence. Since the organisms introduced must be alive, there is the possibility that these may colonize in the animal and produce the disease, and result in abortion
Supply-Agriculture

or permanent infection. Experiments of considerable proportions are under way in regard to this subject, and it is hoped that in the relatively early future this factor in Bang's disease particularly will be clearly understood.
That is the end of the review of what is being done, and the results that have been obtained from the experiments carried on up to date. I may say that the practice of marking animals which have once been found to have Bang's disease was brought into effect the first year I was Minister of Agriculture. They are marked with a "B" in the ear, and anyone who is buying cattle can knew that they have been tested, and that they have shown reaction.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: Would the minister say that the blood test which is made can be relied upon in all cases?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
Yes, we rely upon it in all cases. There may be mistakes occasionally, but it is just as reliable as tests made for tuberculosis.
With regard to mastitis, I may say that experiments are continuing. Our studies with the various chemo-therapeutic agents which have been suggested have not given encouraging results, except when they are used in the very early stages of infection. So far as our studies have advanced they suggest that the control of economic loss from mastitis must be done by sanitary measures, together with chemotherapy in the early infection.
Shipping fever has been given considerable attention in our laboratories. This is a disease which is generally considered as being due to the causative agent of haemorrhagic septicaemia, and appears to have a much wider etiological cause. We suspect, although we have not been able to prove it, that it is associated with a virus. At any rate, we can say that clinically shipping fever is not always due to the causative agent of haemorrhagic septicaemia, and that vaccination with this organism is not a satisfactory method of control. That experience we have had with it up to the present time.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: But it is the only control there is, is it not?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext:
Yes; it is the only control known at the present time.
The other question, as to the spread of disease among live stock, and particularly among hogs, owing to the fact that more farmers are raising hogs, and raising them in greater numbers, is one which is being taken care of, as far as is possible, through cooperation with the provincial authorities. That is to say, we have our men out working on it, and the provincial

authorities have their men. We cover the different rural districts from time to time, and everything which can be done to assist farmers is being done; that is, everything that can be done with the expenditure of money we are now making.
The question as to whether expenditures should be increased is one which is always involved in building up our estimates. During war time we do not think we can spend any more than we are now spending. I quite realize it may be said in answer that probably we would be doing a great deal more for production of meat, and that kind of thing, by that method than by some other method. But there is the difficulty that we have a shortage of qualified men to act in the outlying districts, largely because for a long period of time it has not paid very well for men to take up the studies of a veterinary. The result is that we have not had as many as we could use, particularly with the number of stock spread across Canada. Probably there is not as much being done as might be done in that regard-

speechtext: Is the best treatment for this disease to kill the animal, or can the disease be combated successfully by other means?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: I stated a few moments ago that if the calf vaccine is used early enough, when the animal is from four to six months old, it is possible to check the disease to a certain extent, but as animals get older it is thought best to kill them.

speechtext: Have any other methods of taking care of this disease been discovered?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANSWER TO QUESTION ON FEBRUARY 28
speechtext: We have a Bang's disease control policy, but I repeat that the general idea is that when once an animal is marked as being afflicted with the disease the best thing to do is to kill it. speechtext: My experience has shown that even though diseased animals are cleaned out of the herd, other animals continue to get the disease. Has that been the experience all over Canada?

The minister has stated that one of the means of controlling Bang's disease and hemorrhagic septicaemia is to adopt sanitary measures. There is another question I should like to ask. What laboratory facilities are available in the department at the present time? Where are these laboratories located and how are they manned? I suppose they are manned by veterinary surgeons, but are these men qualified to do research work? I should like a general statement on the laboratory situation throughout the country.

speechtext: The main laboratory dealing with Bang's disease is just across the river in Hull. Then there is one at Lethbridge and one in British Columbia, just outside Victoria. There are pamphlets sent out covering all these things, and they go out by the thousands to farmers all over the country. speechtext: Would the minister make a statement now, or at some later stage when his estimates are before the committee, with reference to this and the other scientific service branches, dealing with their work for the benefit of those members of the committee who are not farmers. As I understand it, these are research branches seeking to gather information in regard to certain animal diseases. How are the results of their researches made available to the farmers? The minister says that literature is sent out. I should like to know on what basis it is sent out. Does the farmer know where to send for it? Is a mailing list kept? Also with regard to vaccines, are they made available to farmers through the provincial departments of agriculture? Going around last fall, I found the live stock producers experiencing contagious abortion among cattle and erysipelas among hogs. The veterinaries were terribly overworked. In the second place I found that many farmers did not know how to go about dealing with that particular situation because some of them had started to raise live stock only since the war began. How do they go .about getting this information? Would the minister tell the committee so that the farmers will know how the results of this research work can be made available to them.

speechtext:
Health, of course,
whether of animals or of human beings, is largely under the control of the provinces, and in most of the provinces they have district representatives who are out covering those areas. That is true in Saskatchewan and elsewhere. These men are very well informed as to all the different treatments that can be given, and then there are, of course, in some districts the veterinarians who are consulted.
Publications are put out in great numbers by the. department in all sections of the country, and there are articles in the local papers which can be read by the farmers, and which give a great deal of information. In the district in which I farm, the best agent is the druggist who handles many of the treatments. He gives more publicity to what can be done and probably gives better service to the farmers than anyone else. He is in the district and keeps track of all treatments that can be used, and he takes the trouble to go among the farmers and indicate what can be done. That, of course, is part of his own business in distributing the things he has to sell. In the different districts it is done in different ways, but most farmers are well informed as to what can be done, where to get information and how to use the different treatments, though, of course, it is like everything else concerning disease; the treatment is not always administered at the right time and is, therefore, not preventive but rather curative.
